Side effects

MOTS-c side effects

MOTS-c has no side-effect data from clinical trials: none has been completed, and FDA's 2026 review found no human safety information.12 What exists are unverified reports summarized by USADA, results from a trial of a related analog, and FDA warnings about immune reactions and product quality.132

What is known in people

FDA's 2026 review found no clinical studies or human exposure data for MOTS-c by any route, so it concluded that the safety risks in humans are unknown.2 It also found no nonclinical toxicity studies, such as repeat-dose, genetic, reproductive or cancer studies.2 USADA states that no human clinical trial has been completed and that there are no data on long-term use.1

So the MOTS-c side effects listed below are not rates from trials. They come from three weaker kinds of evidence: user reports, a trial of a related molecule, and FDA's review of the risks.

At a glance, by seriousness

Concern How serious Evidence behind it
Immune reactions From antibodies with no symptoms to life-threatening reactions FDA concern about aggregates and impurities in injected MOTS-c; user reports include immune reactions21
Effects on organs Unknown No toxicity studies, and the molecular targets are unknown2
Palpitations, insomnia, fever, injection site irritation Not measured Unverified user reports summarized by USADA1
Injection site reactions Short-lived, generally mild to moderate Company trial of the analog CB4211, not MOTS-c3

Reported effects, grouped by source

Unverified reports from people who purchased MOTS-c online

USADA summarizes these effects reported by people who say they purchased MOTS-c online:1

  • Increased heart rate or heart palpitations
  • Irritation at the injection site
  • Insomnia
  • Local or whole-body immune reactions
  • Fever

These are anecdotes, not study results.1 No study has measured how often they occur.2

A company trial of the analog CB4211 (not MOTS-c)

CB4211 is a modified analog of MOTS-c, so its results may not carry over.3 The phase 1a/1b trial enrolled 88 people.4

  • In the 4-week phase 1b part, injection site reactions were the only adverse events seen in more than 10% of treated participants.3 They were short-lived and generally mild to moderate.3
  • The company reported no serious adverse events.3
  • In November 2018 the trial was paused to address mild injection site reactions that had become unexpectedly persistent.5

Risks FDA has flagged

Immune reactions

FDA is concerned that injected MOTS-c may trigger an immune response, because the peptide may form aggregates and may carry peptide-related impurities.2 Such responses can range from antibodies with no symptoms to life-threatening reactions.2 Antibodies could in theory also neutralize the body's own MOTS-c.2 FDA's list of bulk substances that may present significant safety risks names immunogenicity, impurities and characterization problems for MOTS-c.6

Identity and quality

FDA considers MOTS-c free base not well characterized.2 The free base and the acetate salt are different ingredients, and naming that does not follow chemical standards can mean a person receives a different substance than intended.2 Peptides can also clump or degrade with changes in pH, heat, concentration or impurities.2

Unknown organ effects

FDA reviewers say the molecular targets of MOTS-c are unknown, which makes it hard to predict which organs it may affect.2 With no toxicity studies on record, no source describes effects on specific organs at any exposure.2

Why no reports does not mean safe

FDA's adverse event database had no MOTS-c reports in searches through March 9, 2025.2 That absence says little, because compounders generally do not report adverse events to FDA.2 There are also no data on use in pregnancy, in children or alongside other drugs, since FDA found no human exposure data and no reproductive toxicity studies.2

Warnings

  • Sport. MOTS-c is prohibited at all times under section 4.4.1 (activators of AMPK) of the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List.1 USADA says a therapeutic use exemption is highly unlikely because it has no approved therapeutic use.1
  • Long-term use. No data exist on what happens with long-term use.1
  • Approved options. FDA's advisory committee reviewed MOTS-c for obesity and osteoporosis, conditions for which FDA-approved medicines already exist.72
  • General practice. For handling and safety basics that apply to any peptide, see Peptide safety basics.

Frequently asked questions

What are the side effects of MOTS-c?

No controlled study has documented MOTS-c side effects, because no human trial has been completed.1 The available reports are anecdotal.1 USADA's summary of unverified reports from people who say they purchased it online includes palpitations, insomnia, injection site irritation, immune reactions and fever.1 In a small company trial of the related analog CB4211, injection site reactions were the only adverse events seen in more than 10% of treated participants.3

Are MOTS-c peptides safe?

Safety in people is unknown.2 FDA found no human exposure data and no toxicity studies,2 and its list of bulk substances that may present significant safety risks says compounded MOTS-c may pose a significant risk of immune reactions, with complexities around impurities and characterization.6 USADA adds that no human clinical trial has been completed and that there are no data on long-term use.1

Does MOTS-c affect your heart?

Effects on the human heart are unknown.2 In a rat model of blood-vessel calcification, MOTS-c reduced vessel and heart changes.2 In people, studies have only measured the body's own MOTS-c, which was higher in patients with unstable angina or a heart attack in one Chinese study.8 Fast heart rate and palpitations appear in USADA's list of unverified user reports, but no study has examined them.1

Is MOTS-c hard on the liver?

There are no human data on MOTS-c and liver safety, and FDA found no toxicity studies that would show liver effects.2 In mice on a high-fat diet, MOTS-c reduced fat build-up in the liver.2 A company-run 4-week trial of the analog CB4211 reported lower liver enzymes, but CB4211 is a different molecule.3

How does MOTS-c make you feel?

No study has measured how MOTS-c makes people feel, since no human trial has been completed.1 Claims about energy come from marketing, not human data: FDA found injectable MOTS-c sold online for uses such as mitochondrial energy.2 The unverified reports USADA summarized include insomnia and palpitations, and they cannot show how common any effect is.1
